title: Evolving a brain, stage by stage
text:
Introduction
This book follows one experiment: growing a brain in a simulation, one piece at a time, in roughly the order in which brains are thought to have evolved.
Each stage adds a small circuit to the brain of the previous stage, and changes the world so that the new circuit has something to be good for. Evolution then gets a number of generations to put the circuit to use. Each page of this book is one stage: what was added and why, the biology it is modelled on, and whether it worked.
The idea of explaining cognition in steps that follow evolution comes from the book A Brief History of Intelligence by Max Bennett. The stages do not match its chapters one to one, and you do not need to have read it to follow along.
A disclaimer: this work is not guaranteed to be scientifically accurate, and its brains do not match real brains exactly. It stays close to nature where it can, and elsewhere it just “goes for it”: it builds up to something advanced from what works, without a citation for every choice. Still, I think that following these experiments builds an intuition about intelligence that could prove useful both in neuroscience and in machine learning.
New to neurons or to evolutionary algorithms? The background page explains everything this book assumes, with a glossary.

title: Evolving a brain, stage by stage
text:
The creatures and their world
The creatures live on a grid. Each has a stomach that empties a little every tick (one tick is about a second of behaviour), and faster when it moves. A creature whose stomach is empty dies.
Food grows on bushes. Once a bush’s last berry is eaten it stays empty for a long time, longer than a full stomach lasts, so a creature has to keep moving. At any moment only a small share of the bushes carries berries. A bite costs a little energy.
The objects, their names and their pictures come from the game One Hour One Life. The simulation uses a small slice of the game’s rules at each stage, and a larger one as the brain grows.
The creatures wear the bodies of the game’s people, because those are the pictures it has, and the clothes make each one easy to follow. Their brains start out far simpler than a worm’s. This book calls them creatures and keeps the word animal for real ones.
A creature senses the world through a few coarse “eyes”: a handful of directions, in each of which it sees whether something is there, how near it is, and what it looks like. What something looks like is a short list of numbers, its look. It can step forward, turn left or right, and grasp what is in front of it.

title: Evolving a brain, stage by stage
text:
How a stage is judged
Every stage page ends with Did it work?, which answers two questions.

Is the new circuit used? The evolved creatures live again with the new cells silenced, a lesion. If they do clearly worse, in every seed, they were using them. This is the main criterion: a circuit that is used is one that later stages can build on.
Does the new brain do better than the old one? Each stage has a main run, with the new circuit, and a control: the brain of the previous stage, put in the same new world and evolved from the same starting population. The new circuit is the only difference between them. The new brain does not have to win; it must not be clearly worse.

Evolution is noisy: one run can end almost anywhere. So every stage is run three times from different random starts (seeds), and a result counts only when it holds across them. In the charts, bars are the mean and dots are the seeds.
The comparison is measured in two ways. Each among its own kind: every final population lives again in the same set of worlds, so that no population owes its score to easier worlds. Sharing one world: half new and half old creatures live together and compete for the same bushes. When the two disagree, the page says why.
The fitness that all of this measures is the well-fed lifetime: how long a creature lived from its first meal, with each tick weighted by how full its stomach was.
Under Full results, each page keeps everything else, folded away: fitness over the generations, every measure with its standard error, every lesion, and what did not work. The results table there has up to three rows: the last generations as they ran, each among its own kind, and sharing one world (head to head). The lesion chart has one bar per region: fitness with that region silenced, as a percentage of the intact population.

title: Evolving a brain, stage by stage
section: How to read a stage page
text:
How to read a stage page
A page starts with a short summary box, the brain diagram and the new circuit. Where it helps, a Watching it work strip follows one creature over a few dozen ticks, so that you can see the circuit act. Then come the biology the stage is modelled on, the world it was tested in, and Did it work?. At the end, Runs links to a dashboard that replays the last generation of a run.
The diagrams and charts show more when you point at a box, an arrow, a bar or a curve, or tap it on a phone. The numbers, graphs and diagrams are drawn from data files written when a stage is run; only the text is written by hand.

title: Background
text:
Neurons and synapses
Brains and evolution in brief
This book assumes no biology and little machine learning. This page explains the few ideas that every later page uses: what a neuron does, why some neurons excite and others inhibit, how to read the brain diagrams, the three ways a connection gets its strength, and how evolution and the experiments are run. The parts of real brains that the stages model are introduced on their own pages. A glossary at the end collects the terms.
If you already know neural networks, the callout below says what is different here.
A neuron is a cell that collects signals from other neurons and passes on a signal of its own. In this book a neuron is described by one number, its activity: 0 when it is silent, 1 when it fires as fast as it can.
Neurons are connected by synapses. A synapse has a strength (in machine learning: a weight). Every tick, a neuron adds up the activity of the neurons that reach it, each multiplied by the strength of its synapse, and its new activity follows that sum, squashed into the range from 0 to 1 (a negative sum gives 0). That is nearly all of it.
The words neuron and cell mean the same thing in this book.

title: Background
text:
Exciting and inhibiting
A synapse can push its target up or down. An excitatory neuron raises the activity of every neuron it reaches; an inhibitory neuron lowers it. A real neuron is one or the other, never both (this is called Dale’s law), and the brains in this book follow that rule.
Inhibition is not just “the minus sign”. It is how a brain says not now, and most of the circuits in this book are built from three small patterns:


  
  
  A
  B
  Excitation
  A fires, so B fires
  
  
  
  E
  G
  B
  A gate
  E drives B, but the inhibitory
  gate G holds it shut
  
  
  
  
  E
  X
  G
  B
  Disinhibition
  X silences the gate,
  so B is released

Filled circles fire, pale circles are silent; red-edged circles are inhibitory. An arrowhead
excites its target, a bar inhibits it.


Excitation passes a signal on: this is food, so bite.
A gate is an inhibitory cell that holds an action back until a condition is met. In the valence stage, a cell that fires whenever nothing is within reach holds the bite shut, so that wanting to eat does not turn into biting the air.
Disinhibition switches a gate off, and that releases the action. Brains use it a lot: rather than pushing an action into being, they keep many actions held back and lift the hold on one.

A fourth pattern appears later: competition, where cells inhibit each other so that only the strongest few stay active.

title: Background
text:
Reading a brain diagram
Every stage page shows the brain of that stage. Here is the brain of the valence stage, the second one:




A box is a group of neurons with one job, called a region: the eyes, the motor neurons that move the creature, a cell for pain. Its name says what it is for.
An arrow between two boxes is a projection: all the synapses from one region onto another. The end of the arrow says what it does: an arrowhead excites, a bar inhibits, and a dot (on arrows from the senses) means a mix of both.
The colour of an arrow says where its strengths come from (next section), and its width how strong it is overall.
Under a box’s name: whether its cells excite or inhibit, and how many there are. The coloured backgrounds group regions that belong together.
A box outlined in green is new in this stage. The diagram opens on the new circuit: what the stage added and what it connects to directly, with the groups it does not touch drawn as empty outlines. All cells shows the other cells too, faded; everything shows the whole brain.

Point at a box or an arrow, or tap it on a phone, for details. You do not need to follow every arrow. Each page says in words which arrows matter, and the rest is the brain of earlier stages.

title: Background
text:
Where strengths come from









arrow
origin
changes
example




dark
designed (hard-wired): we wire it, evolution may only make it stronger or weaker as a whole
over generations, as a whole
pain → the “this is bad” cells


grey
evolved: which synapses exist and how strong each is is inherited, with mutations
over generations, synapse by synapse
eyes → motor neurons


purple

within one life
the look of a berry → “this is bad”, after it hurt



Designed connections give a cell a fixed meaning that later stages can rely on: a cell that is wired to pain and nothing else means pain. Evolved connections are where evolution finds its own solutions, often in ways that are hard to read. Learned connections are the only memory a creature has of its own life.

Learning within a life
The learning in this book follows one recipe, found in real animals from sea slugs to mammals. A synapse that was just active leaves a short trace. When something important happens, such as pain, a teaching signal is sent to many synapses at once, and only the ones that carry a trace change. Pain says something bad happened; the trace says and this is what was there.


Modulators
Some cells do not talk to one partner through a synapse. They release a neuromodulator, a substance that spreads and reaches many cells at once, and that is cleared slowly. Serotonin and dopamine are the best-known. Modulators set the mood of a brain more than its next move: because they linger, they let an event act on behaviour for a while after it is over. In the diagrams they are drawn in pink.

title: Background
text:
Evolution
Evolution here is a genetic algorithm. A genome is what a creature inherits: the strengths of its evolved synapses and a few settings, such as how fast it learns. A population of genomes is born into a world, each as a few identical creatures. The fitness of a genome is how well its creatures did: here, roughly, how long they lived with a full stomach. The genomes that did best have children, each from two parents, with small random changes (mutations). That is one generation, and a stage runs for about a hundred of them.
Nobody tells evolution what a circuit is for. If a new cell helps, the genomes that use it have more children; if it does not, evolution may turn it down or ignore it.

title: Background
text:
Reading the experiments
Each stage asks one question: does the new circuit get used? Three tools answer it.

Main against control. Main is the new brain. The control is the brain of the previous stage, in the same new world, starting from the same population. Whatever separates them is the new circuit, so every comparison on a stage page is new brain against old brain.
Lesions. At the end, a region of the evolved brain is silenced and the creatures live again. If they do much worse, they were using it. This is the main evidence on every page.
Seeds. Evolution is noisy: one run can end almost anywhere. So every stage is run three times from different random starts (seeds). A result counts only when it holds in all three.

Results are given as a mean over the seeds with a standard error (±): roughly, how far the mean might move if the experiment were run again. A difference smaller than about twice its standard error could be luck. How a stage is judged on the introduction page says more.

a cell that triggers a whole action, such as biting

title: Roadmap
text:
Chapter 1: steering
This page says where the book is going. The first chapter is written and the second has begun. Everything after that is a plan, and the plan changes as the experiments come in: stages have already been moved, merged and left out, and that will happen again.
The order follows the five breakthroughs of A Brief History of Intelligence. Each is one chapter, each belongs to a group of animals, and each builds on the brain of the chapter before it.
The brain of a small worm. It turns what it sees into movement (Steering), sorts the world into good and bad (Valence), stops reacting to what is always there (Habituation), learns in one life which new foods hurt (Association), looks after hunger and cold (Drives), and stays in a state for a while after a meal or a poison bite, a state that builds up over several bites (Affect). Last, a region with random wiring spreads the look of a thing out over many cells, so that things that look alike can still be told apart, even when only a combination of features says which is which (Pallium). Insects have such a region, the mushroom body; in vertebrates it is the oldest part of the pallium.
This creature learns one thing: what to stay away from, taught by pain. It cannot learn what is worth going to, it cannot unlearn, and it cannot learn what to do.

title: Roadmap
text:
Chapter 2: reinforcing
The brain of an early fish. The first vertebrates hunted in open water, and nearly all the parts of the vertebrate brain were already there. What they add is learning from surprise: the difference between what happened and what was expected. This chapter adds the parts in the following order.

Dopamine (Critic). A cell that fires when things turn out better than expected, and falls silent when they turn out worse. With it the creature learns what predicts food, and what predicts the thing that predicts food. It also learns to like, and to unlearn, which chapter 1 could not do.
Hands and the basal ganglia (Actor). Until here the creature eats what it grasps. Now it can pick something up, hold it, and eat it or put it down, so that the same action means different things. The basal ganglia’s actor, taught by the same dopamine signal, chooses between them. In this world evolution made most of the actor’s choice innate; learning which action pays, as a rat learns to press a lever, needs a world where a wrong action costs something the critic can see, or a sense of time lost.
Curiosity. New things become a little rewarding in themselves, so that the creature tries what it does not know yet.
The hippocampus. A map of places, made from the creature’s sense of its own movement and from landmarks, so that it can learn where food is, not only what it looks like, and go back there when it is out of sight. It comes after the basal ganglia: a map is of use only to a creature that can learn which way to turn at a place. Goldfish without this part of the pallium can still learn to swim to a marker, but no longer to a place.

Parked until these work: precise timing (the cerebellum), and modulators that set how fast the creature learns when its world is steady or changing.
Two things change in how the stages are done. The circuits are designed and tested before any evolution, and evolution then tunes them, in fewer generations than in chapter 1. And the learning stages get lab experiments: one creature in a scripted situation, as in an animal lab, to see whether it learns the way real animals do.

title: Roadmap
text:
Chapter 3: simulating
The brain of an early mammal, and its new part, the neocortex. The cortex learns to predict what the creature will sense next. Once it can do that, it can be run without the world: the creature stops at a choice, plays out each option, and picks the one that ends best.
The planned stages: a cortex that predicts, trying actions in the head at a choice point, routes stored on the map of chapter 2 and replayed during rest and sleep, holding a goal through distractions, and remembering a single event.
The tests are the classic ones from the rat lab. An animal that explored a maze without reward goes straight to food that appears there later. An animal whose path is blocked takes a detour. An animal that has had enough of one food stops working for it at once.

title: Roadmap
text:
Chapter 4: mentalizing
The brain of a primate, living in a group in which the others matter. The brain first gets a model of itself: what it knows, and how sure it is. Applied to another creature, the same model says what that creature wants and what it has seen.
The planned stages: knowing when it does not know, reading the goals of others, learning a skill by watching, and preparing for a need it does not feel yet, such as storing food before the winter.

title: Roadmap
text:
Chapter 5: speaking
The human step. Calls with a fixed meaning come first, then signals whose meaning is agreed on within a group, then naming what two creatures are both looking at. The aim at the end is knowledge that no single life could find again and that still grows from one generation to the next.
This chapter is the least certain, both in what is known about evolution and in whether a small grid world can carry it.

title: Roadmap
text:
The world grows too
A brain can only be tested on what its world asks of it, so the world grows with the brain. It takes more and more of the rules of One Hour One Life: tools, fire and cooking, and chains of steps that are too long to find by accident. Animals that move by themselves come in as prey and as predators.
For the last two chapters, the way lives are run has to change as well. A generation now starts and ends together. Creatures that watch, imitate and teach each other need parents, children and lives that overlap.

title: Steering
text:
The circuit
Turning sight into movement
The first creature has no memory, no hunger and no idea of good or bad. It can do one thing: turn what it sees into movement. This stage evolves a brain that does that, starting from random wiring. Everything after this stage is added to this brain.
You do not need to follow the arrows. Every synapse here is evolved: which ones exist and how strong they are. Nothing is designed, nothing changes during a life, and no neuron has a meaning you could name. On later pages the ganglion is drawn as a single box.
The brain sees the outside world only. It does not feel its stomach and does not notice whether a bite gave it anything; those senses enter in later stages, through cells made for them.

title: Steering
text:
A ganglion: sixteen excitatory and eight inhibitory neurons (ganglion_e and ganglion_i). The eyes connect to it, its neurons connect to each other, and it connects to the motor neurons.
Reflex arcs: direct connections from the eyes to the motor neurons.

title: Steering
text:
Watching it work
One creature from the last generation, walking up to a bush and eating. The rows below the picture are the neurons of the ganglion. There is nothing in them to read, and that is the point: the behaviour is spread over all of them, wherever evolution happened to put it.

title: Steering
text:
Biology
The oldest animals with a front and a back were small worms, and what set them apart from jellyfish and sponges was that they could go somewhere. A body with a front end, senses on it and a clump of neurons behind them can turn towards what is good and away from what is bad. In A Brief History of Intelligence this is the first breakthrough, steering.
In the worm C. elegans, with 302 neurons, sensory neurons connect to a few layers of interneurons and those to the motor neurons, with some sensory neurons wired to motor neurons directly. A direct connection is a reflex. The interneurons in between let several senses be weighed against each other before the muscles move.

title: Steering
text:
The world
Four kinds of berry bush and wild onions. Everything is food and nothing is dangerous. Moving costs energy, so an creature that stands still starves, and so does one that walks without getting anywhere. The only way to live is to reach a bush with berries, bite, and go on to the next one.

title: Steering
text:
Did it work?



The creatures depend on their ganglion: without it they keep less than a fifth of their fitness. The direct reflex arcs alone are far from enough. There is no old brain to compare with, so this stage was run once: every later stage starts from this one population.

title: Steering
text:
Full results






NoteFitness over the generations





The jump in the curve is a change of setting, not of brain: the population first evolved in short lives and was then given lives four times as long, as in every later stage. In a long life a creature that eats once and then stands still does not reach the end, and over the following generations the standing still is selected away.












NoteAll fitness measures

















NoteAll lesions

















NoteWhat did not work: all the food at once





In earlier runs every bush was full when the creatures were born. They filled their stomachs early and kept eating, the bushes were stripped by the middle of the life, and since a bush takes long to regrow most creatures then starved together. Whatever a creature might have done better later in life could not show.
Starting most bushes empty, each at a random point of its regrowth, turned that stock into a steady flow: the share of bushes with berries stays about the same through a life.

title: Valence
text:
The circuit
Good and bad
The creature of the previous stage steers by reflex. What it sees is wired, through a small ganglion, straight to its motor neurons, and it cannot tell what happened after it bit something.
This stage gives it cells for good and bad, a sorting of the world that is called valence. The world gets something to sort: two kinds of berry are now poison, and a poison bite hurts.
Point at or tap a box or an arrow for details. Dark arrows are designed, grey ones evolved; see reading a brain diagram.
Five new groups of cells, each with a meaning fixed by its wiring:
Good leads to a bite, but only when the food is in reach. The good cells excite grasp, and no_touch holds it shut until something is directly ahead. This is disinhibition, the release of an action by switching off its gate (background).
Bad turns the creature away and stops the bite, as in a worm that touches something harmful: the bad cells drive the turning motor neurons, and through no_feed they shut down biting.
The eyes give the value cells a head start. Taste and pain arrive only after a bite. So the value cells also get input from the eyes, and that input is evolved. Over the generations, the look of a poison berry comes to excite the bad cells before anything has been eaten.

title: Valence
text:
valence_app, good: the sense of taste is wired to these cells, and reaches the brain nowhere else.
valence_av, bad: pain is wired to these cells, and reaches the brain nowhere else.
grasp: when it fires, the creature bites what is in front of it.
no_touch, a gate: fires whenever nothing is within reach, and holds grasp shut.
no_feed: driven by the bad cells, it blocks the bite.

title: Valence
text:
Watching it work
One creature from the last generation, around the moment it bites a poison berry. Step through it one tick at a time.
At the bite nothing has changed yet: the pain arrives one tick later. Then pain is on, both bad cells fire, no_feed switches on and grasp falls silent. The creature turns away. A few ticks later the pain has faded and it is eating again.



Nothing was learned here: the creature will react the same way next time. What keeps it from biting poison often is the evolved input from the eyes, which acts before the bite.

title: Valence
text:
Biology
In small animals most sensory neurons fall into two classes: some respond to things worth approaching, such as the smell of food, others to things worth avoiding, such as a harmful chemical. The two classes converge on a few interneurons that bias the animal towards carrying on or turning away.
In the worm C. elegans, with 302 neurons, a harmful stimulus does two things at once: it triggers a turn, and it stops the pumping of the throat with which the worm feeds. Max Bennett argues that this sorting into good and bad is what the first brains were for.
The worm is a stand-in. The animal this chapter is about, the common ancestor of all animals with a left and a right side, left no nervous system to look at.

title: Valence
text:
The world
Six kinds of berry bush instead of four, each with its own colour. Four are food. Two are poison, and always the same two: a poison berry empties the stomach by about as much as a good berry fills it, and it hurts for a moment.
Because the poison kinds never change, nothing has to be learned within a life: which colours to avoid can be inherited. Learning it within a life comes in a later stage.

title: Valence
text:
Did it work?



Look at the first two bars: without the bad cells, or without no_feed, the creatures keep only about a tenth of their fitness. The good side matters much less, because the reflexes of the previous stage already bring the creature to food and make it bite.
The old brain falls far behind. It cannot feel pain, so it can avoid poison only if evolution happens to wire “this colour, turn away” into its reflexes, and in the generations given it did not.
That says how much easier the value cells make the solution to find, not what pain is worth in principle: the poison looks the same in every generation, and a brain without pain could evolve the same avoidance by colour. In earlier runs with many more generations, two of three controls eventually did, late and suddenly.
The difference shows in how the creatures spend their lives:

title: Valence
text:
Full results






NoteFitness over the generations





The three main curves do not rise at the same moment: when evolution finds the wiring from the look of the poison kinds to the bad cells is a matter of luck. One seed found it within a few generations; the other two were still climbing when the planned generations were over, and were given as many again.












NoteAll fitness measures








What the three rows measure: see how a stage is judged.









NoteAll lesions

















NoteHow a life is spent

















NoteWhat did not work: appetite on a full stomach





In the first runs of this stage the creatures were born with a full stomach, and the good side was not used at all. A full stomach lasted most of a life, so there was little to gain from eating well. Born a quarter full, the creatures use it a little.
One fault remains: the good side makes the creature bite whenever food is in reach, hungry or not, and many bites land on a nearly full stomach. Nothing in this brain can sense the stomach yet; a later stage adds a cell for hunger.

title: Habituation
text:
The circuit
Getting used to what is always there
The creatures of the previous stage respond to a look in the same way every time they see it. An emptied bush still looks enough like food, so a creature can stand in front of it for a long time, biting. A creature should stop responding to something that stays the same and keeps giving nothing.
This stage changes one thing, in the eyes: they get used to what they keep seeing. To make that worth having, the world gets a dud, a bush that looks like food and never carries a berry.
No new cells. Each of the eyes’ look inputs keeps a slow average of what it has seen over roughly the last fifty ticks, and passes on only the difference between what it sees now and that average.
Every neuron downstream of the eyes now gets this adapted look, and two things follow:

title: Habituation
text:
What stays in view fades. A creature standing in front of a bush sees its look sink into the average. The good cells, driven by that look, fall silent, and with them the urge to bite. The creature moves on.
What is unusual stands out. All berry bushes look alike in most respects, and that shared part is nearly always in the average. What passes through is the part that differs: the colour of this bush. Nothing uses this yet; the next stage does.

title: Habituation
text:
Watching it work
One creature from the last generation, at a dud. The two vis+0 rows are two look inputs of the eye that points straight ahead (vis for vision, +0 for its direction).
The creature walks up and bites. The dud does not change, yet what the eye reports sinks a little with every tick. The good cells and grasp hold for a while, then drop out, and the biting stops. When the creature turns away, the look inputs go below zero: the eye is still used to the dud and reports less of that look than usual.

title: Habituation
text:
Biology
Step into a room with a strong smell and after a few minutes it is gone. The smell is still there; the receptors have stopped reporting it. Sensory neurons respond to change, and a steady input carries no news. This is sensory adaptation.
Habituation is the same thing seen in behaviour. A snail that is touched pulls in its horns; touch it again and again and it stops bothering. It is the simplest kind of learning, found in every animal that has been tested, including ones with a few hundred neurons.

title: Habituation
text:
The world
The world of the previous stage with one more kind of bush, the dud: it looks like a berry bush and never carries a berry. Its colour is drawn anew for every life, so nothing an ancestor knew can tell a creature to leave it alone. When the dud happens to have an attractive colour, a creature whose eyes do not adapt will stand at it and bite for as long as it lives.

title: Habituation
text:
Did it work?
There is no group of neurons to silence here, since the change is in how the inputs work. The matching test is to switch the adaptation off in the evolved creatures and let them live again.



The creatures rely on it heavily: without adaptation they keep well under half their fitness. Against the old brain the gain is smaller and uneven across seeds. The control’s fitness swings from one generation to the next, depending on whether it happens to like the colour of that generation’s dud.
The clearest difference is in how a life is spent. Creatures whose eyes adapt stand and bite at nothing less than half as often:

title: Habituation
text:
Full results






NoteFitness over the generations





The first generations of main are a step back. Every inherited synapse was tuned to eyes that reported the whole look, and the eyes now report only the difference, so the population has to re-tune before the change pays.












NoteAll fitness measures








The head-to-head test is left out here: in it all creatures share one set of eyes, and the eyes are the difference.









NoteAdaptation switched off

















NoteAll lesions

















NoteHow a life is spent

















NoteWhat did not work: unfamiliar food





Without the dud, adaptation was used only a little: the long lives had already selected most of the standing still away, and evolution can learn the look of an empty bush of every kind it has always known. Giving the good berries a new colour in every life did not change that. What makes adaptation worth having is something that looks like food and gives nothing, whatever colour it has.

title: Habituation
text: Runs

title: Association
text:
The circuit
Learning what is bad
Until now everything the creature knows was put there by evolution. That works for poison that looks the same in every generation, but not for food that is new. In this stage all food is new: every kind of berry gets a new colour in every life, and which kinds are poison is drawn anew.
One new cell, and one change to existing synapses:
Nothing else has to change. The bad cells already turn the creature away and block the bite, so once the look of a berry excites them, the creature treats that berry like the poison it was born knowing.

title: Association
text:
us_pain, the teacher, is driven by pain alone. When it fires, it sends a teaching signal. (US stands for unconditioned stimulus: something that matters without any learning, as pain does.)
The synapses from the look onto the bad cells (valence_av) can now change during a life. A synapse grows when its input was just active and the teacher fires. These are the purple arrows in the diagram.



What gets the blame
A bite hurts, and something has to take the blame. Getting this right was most of the work of this stage:

The lesson is about what sets the food apart. If pain strengthened the whole look, one bad red berry would make the creature wary of every berry. Here the adapting eyes of the previous stage pay a second time: what all bushes share cancels out before it reaches a synapse, and what is left to take the blame is the colour.
The pain is brief. When pain lasted several ticks, the teacher was still firing after the creature had turned to the next bush, and it learned to distrust the neighbour as much as the poison.
Every learnable synapse exists. A synapse that is not there cannot learn, so all of them are present, the new ones starting at zero.

title: Association
text:
Watching it work
One creature from the last generation, at two moments of its life. First, its first bite of a kind that is poison in this life. Before the bite the bad cells are silent and grasp fires. One tick later the pain arrives, the teacher fires, and the bad cells and no_feed switch on by reflex, as before this stage. What cannot be seen is the change the teacher leaves in the synapses.



Later in the same life the creature comes up to a bush of the same kind. Nothing hurts now, and yet the bad cells fire and no_feed holds the bite back. The creature moves on. It learned this; no ancestor could have told it.

title: Association
text:
Biology
A sea slug that is shocked after a touch learns to pull back from the touch. A rat that gets sick after a new food avoids that food afterwards. This is associative learning: something neutral (the touch, the taste) comes to predict something that matters (the shock, the sickness), and the animal responds to the first as it would to the second.
At the level of synapses, worked out in the sea slug Aplysia and the fruit fly, it has three parts. A sensory neuron that was just active leaves a short trace at its synapses. A teaching signal, released when something bad happens, reaches many synapses at once. Only the synapses with a fresh trace are strengthened. The circuit above is this picture in its simplest form.

title: Association
text:
The world
Four kinds of berry bush, all new in every life: each life draws a new colour for every kind, and which two of the four are poison. The bushes still look like berry bushes; a new kind differs from the others in colour, the way a new berry is still recognisably a berry.
Half of all bushes are poison, so a creature that cannot learn pays on every second bush it tries, all its life. Leaving everything unknown alone is not an option either: there is nothing else to eat.

title: Association
text:
Did it work?



Learning carries this stage. Silence the teacher, or freeze every synapse at its inherited strength, and the creatures keep less than half their fitness. The old brain feels pain and turns away from it, but cannot change, so it pays for every poison bush it tries, every time.
The learners still lead short lives: half of what they try is poison until they have learned it, and nothing yet tells a creature that it is getting hungry.

title: Association
text:
Full results






NoteFitness over the generations

















NoteAll fitness measures

















NoteAll lesions





Learning switched off freezes every synapse at its inherited strength; us_pain silences the teacher.












NoteHow a life is spent

















NoteWhat did not work: unlearning by tasting again





An earlier design had a second cell that lowered the aversion whenever something distrusted turned out to taste fine. It worked when meals were fed to the brain in a test. In a living creature it never fired: aversion blocks the bite, so food that is distrusted is never tasted again, and the mistake is never found out. That is why the lesson has to land on the right food in the first place.









NoteWhat did not work: a world where learning was hardly worth it





The first versions of this world kept a familiar, safe kind of berry as half of all bushes. A creature that learned nothing got by very well, and a perfect learner would have gained less than a tenth of its food. With so little to win, evolution switched learning off whenever a lesson had any side effect. Removing the familiar food turned this around.

title: Association
text: Runs

title: Drives
text:
The circuit
Hunger and cold
Until now the brain has only looked outward. It sees, tastes and feels pain, but has no idea how full its stomach is or how warm its body is, so these creatures forage whether they are starving or stuffed.
This stage makes the world cold, which gives the body a second need, and gives the brain two cells that report on the body: one for a cold skin, one for an emptying stomach.
Four new cells:
The creature has no map of where it is warm. It keeps walking while it is cold and stops where it is warm, and that is enough to end up near warmth most of the time.
These connections are designed; evolution tunes their strength. One set is left entirely to evolution: synapses from hungry onto the cells that feed. They start at zero, so that evolution can build “bite less on a full stomach” if it pays.

title: Drives
text:
cold fires while the skin is cold.
warm_seek, driven by cold, pushes the creature forward: keep moving while it is cold.
rest, an inhibitory cell, fires while the skin is warm and holds the forward step back: stay where it is warm.
hungry, an inhibitory cell, fires when the stomach is less than about two-thirds full and shuts both warm_seek and rest. A hungry creature forgets about warmth and forages; a fed one looks after its temperature.

title: Drives
text:
Watching it work
One creature from the last generation, with a full stomach, walking in the cold until it reaches the warmth of a hot spring.
While the skin is cold, cold and warm_seek fire and the creature steps forward every tick. Next to the spring the skin sense rises, cold and warm_seek fall silent, and rest switches on. The creature stays put. hungry stays silent because the stomach is full, so warmth comes first. Towards the end it begins to stir, and rest begins to fade.

title: Drives
text:
Biology
A drive is a signal from the body about something it needs: food, water, warmth, sleep. In vertebrates these signals are gathered in the hypothalamus, where small groups of neurons read the blood and the body and fire when a need is not met. They do not move a muscle themselves; they switch behaviours on and hold others back.
The way these creatures find warmth is older still. A bacterium or a worm in a bad place does not know where the good place is. It moves, and when things are good it stops moving. This is kinesis: no map, only a rule about when to keep going.

title: Drives
text:
The world
The world of the previous stage, made cold. A cold body burns its food faster, so a creature that stays cold starves sooner. A few hot springs warm the ground around them. The creature cannot see where it is warm; it feels only the temperature of its own skin. The food is as before: four kinds of berry bush, new in every life, half of them poison.

title: Drives
text:
Did it work?



The circuit is used, hungry most of all. Silencing hungry does not make the creature less hungry: it removes the one signal that tells the warmth cells to stand down, so the creature rests in the warmth while its stomach empties. cold and warm_seek form one chain and are used least.
Against the old brain, the two measures disagree, and that is a finding. Living among their own kind, the creatures with drives do about as well as the old brain or better. Sharing a world with the old brain, they fall behind: clearly in two seeds, level in the third. They do not get more food; they move less, and a warm body burns food more slowly. A resting creature leaves the bushes around it to whoever is still walking, and in a shared world that is the old brain. Food is scarce enough for this to matter.



So sharing a world measures who wins the race for berries, and resting is a poor way to win a race. It does not show that resting is a mistake for the creature that does it.

title: Drives
text:
Full results






NoteFitness over the generations

















NoteAll fitness measures








Either population alone, in a world with half as many creatures, does far better than at full numbers: food is a race. Inside the populations with the circuit, evolution left the strength of rest where it was designed and made the hunger gate stronger.









NoteAll lesions

















NoteHow a life is spent

title: Drives
text: Runs

title: Affect
text:
The circuit
States that last
Everything this brain does so far, it does about the present. A bush is in front of it, so it bites; the skin is cold, so it walks. When the cause is gone, the behaviour is gone in the same moment.
But some events say something about the minutes that follow. A creature that has just eaten well is probably on good ground; one that has just been hurt is probably on bad ground. To use that, the brain has to keep something of the event after it is over. So that the states have something to work with, the bushes in this world grow in patches that are mostly of one kind.
Two modulators (substances that a few cells release and that reach many cells at once, drawn in pink) and three new cells:
hungry still shuts rest. So a fed creature stays on good ground until it is hungry again, and then forages with good bushes close by.
The states build up. A modulator is released in small amounts and cleared slowly, so its level is a running sum of what happened lately. The cells that read it fire only above a threshold: one poison bite passes without alarm, the creature flees only after more than one; it settles only after more good bites than one bush can give. One bite says little about the ground, several bites close together say much more.
The wiring and thresholds are designed. Evolution tunes the strengths, the thresholds, and how fast each modulator is cleared, which sets how long each state lasts.

title: Affect
text:
Alarm. Pain releases the modulator alarm, which drives flee: the creature keeps going forward for a while, out of the poisoned ground.
Contentment. fed fires when the creature tastes food and releases serotonin, which drives settle, which switches on rest (the cell of the previous stage that holds the forward step back). After a good meal the creature stays where it ate.

title: Affect
text:
Watching it work
One creature from the last generation at a poison bush. It bites three times in a row, and each bite adds to alarm (the row is full at the level where flee begins to fire). One bite is not enough. After the third, flee switches on and the creature walks away, every tick. The alarm is cleared slowly, so the flight outlasts the pain by more than ten ticks.

title: Affect
text:
Biology
A drive, as in the previous stage, follows the body: the hunger cell fires as long as the stomach is empty. An affective state is different in one respect: something sets it off, and then it stays for a while by itself.
In small animals such states are carried by neuromodulators, released quickly and cleared slowly; that slowness is the memory. The worm C. elegans slows down and stays put for minutes after it has found food, under the influence of serotonin. After a harmful touch it speeds away and keeps going well after the touch has ended.
Such a state has two sides: it is good or bad, and it makes the creature more active or less. Alarm is bad and active; contentment is good and quiet.

title: Affect
text:
The world
The bushes now grow in patches, mostly of one kind: after good meals the neighbouring bushes are probably good, after poison bites probably poison. Not every bush in a patch is of the patch’s kind, so knowing a bush by its look, the lesson of the association stage, still has a job.
The world is also four times larger for the same number of creatures, with more food, so that creatures take less food from each other and what a better forager gains is not hidden. The next stage keeps this world. The rest is as before: cold, hot springs, and four kinds of berry bush, new in every life, half of them poison.

title: Affect
text:
Did it work?



Both states are used in every seed. flee costs the most when silenced: in these mixed patches a run of poison bites is the clearest sign of bad ground.
Against the old brain the gain is clear when the two share a world, in every seed. Living apart, two seeds are ahead and one is behind, so that measure alone would be inconclusive.

title: Affect
text:
Full results






NoteFitness over the generations

















NoteAll fitness measures

















NoteAll lesions, and what is not used here








rest, through which both staying after a meal and staying in the warmth act, costs more than fed or settle.
Two older circuits are not used in this world:

cold and warm_seek. A fed creature that walks off in search of warmth leaves the good ground; staying where the food is turns out to be worth more.
Learning. In these patches the look of a bush and the ground it stands on say much the same thing, and the creatures lean on the ground: two poison bites and the alarm carries them off. The learning rate is still there in every seed. What keeps learning from paying is that a lesson about one berry spreads to the berries that look like it, the problem the next stage takes on.

Neither was removed: the next stages need the learning.









NoteAfter a bite








After poison bites the creatures take a few more steps than the old brain, after a good meal a few fewer. The differences are small in this measure because one bite alone no longer sets a state off.









NoteHow a life is spent








Both populations stand still for most of their life, much of it biting at nothing: a creature held in place by rest still has its grasp programme, and a bite costs little.

title: Affect
text: Runs

title: Pallium
text:
The circuit
Telling look-alikes apart
Since the association stage the creature learns from pain which bushes to avoid, on the look of a bush: a handful of colour features. That works when poison and good food differ in some feature. It fails when what makes a bush poison is a combination: here a bush is poison when its two colour features are both high or both low, and good when one is high and the other low. Whatever a lesson on the features teaches about one poison, it teaches the opposite about the other.
This stage adds a new region in front of the learning, the pallium.
Only the eye ahead feeds the pallium: at a bite, the side eyes see neighbouring bushes, and those would be blamed too. A creature turns to a bush before it bites it, so the eye ahead sees the one that counts.

title: Pallium
text:
pallium: 128 cells. Each reads the colour features of the eye that points straight ahead, through synapses of random strength. The wiring is random and evolution does not shape it: what matters is that every cell is different, not what each one is.
Few cells at a time. Only the two cells that receive the most input fire; the others are held silent. (Real brains do this with inhibitory cells that every active cell excites; the model takes the shortcut and keeps the strongest two, called k-winners-take-all.) Because so few cells fire, two kinds of bush that share most of their look share almost none of their active cells.
The lesson. Pain teaches the synapses from the pallium onto the bad cells, by the same rule that has taught the synapses from the look since the association stage. The old route stays and still learns too; evolution sets how fast each route learns.

title: Pallium
text:
Biology
Insects and vertebrates both have a region built for telling look-alikes apart. In the insect mushroom body, about fifty smell channels fan out onto thousands of cells, a few percent of which fire, held down by a single inhibitory cell that all of them excite; dopamine cells then teach the synapses at its output what each pattern means. The vertebrate pallium, the roof of the forebrain (in mammals most of it became the cerebral cortex), has the same design in its oldest part, the piriform cortex: every cell receives input from a random handful of smell channels, and only a few percent of the cells respond to any one smell. Such a random, sparse expansion separates inputs that overlap, which is why a fly can learn to avoid one smell and not its look-alike.
Whether the two are one invention is open. The mushroom bodies of marine worms are built from the same set of genes as the vertebrate pallium, which suggests that a common, worm-like ancestor already had such a region; insects and vertebrates may also have arrived at it twice. Either way the design is old and simple, and in this book it closes the first chapter: it is still taught by pain alone, as in the association stage. It keeps the vertebrate name, pallium, because the later stages build on it.
A creature turns to a bush before it bites it, so the eye ahead stands for the part of the senses that an animal points at its food. That the first such region did this job for vision, and not only for smell, is a guess of the model.

title: Pallium
text:
The world
The world of the affect stage, with two changes. The four new kinds of bush in every life have looks on the corners of a square, as in the figure above. And the patches are mixed: every patch holds every kind, so where a bush grows says nothing about what it is, and the look has to do the job.

title: Pallium
text:
Did it work?



The pallium is used in every seed. Switching off all learning costs more than the pallium alone, because the look still learns as well. Against the old brain, the new brain is ahead in every seed when the two share a world. Measured apart, one seed is level: one life per creature makes that measure noisy.

In the lab
The sharpest test is outside the world. One creature at a time eats from four new bushes, two poison and two good, twice each, and is then shown each bush again. How likely is it to bite?



Learning on the look alone makes the creature shy of all four bushes alike: it cannot tell the kinds apart. Learning through the pallium alone more than halves the bites at poison and leaves the good bushes almost untouched. With both routes learning, as in the world, the creature is shy of the good bushes too, but less than of the poison.

title: Pallium
text:
Full results






NoteFitness over the generations

















NoteAll fitness measures

















NoteAll lesions








Of the states of the affect stage only the one that settles the creature at food is still used, a little; fleeing and being fed no longer matter. In mixed patches the place says little about a bush; its look says more.









NoteThe lab in numbers

















NoteWhat it took






Mixed patches. In patches of mostly one kind, the place answered the question first: a poison bite or two and the alarm carried the creature off, and knowing a poison by its look saved only the first bite at the next bush of that kind. Evolution then turned the lessons down.
Fewer cells at a time. With four cells active instead of two, a lesson spread twice as far to the good bushes.
Evolution still damps aversion close up. In every population the inputs that see a bush right ahead hold the bad cells down: approach what is in front of you. A lesson has to overcome that before it can stop a bite.

From this stage on, how strongly the look inputs adapt (the habituation stage) is set by evolution too.

title: Pallium
text: Runs

title: Critic
text:
The circuit
Learning from surprise
So far pain has been the teacher. Every painful bite strengthens the aversion to what the creature was looking at, and nothing weakens it again. That works as long as the world keeps its promises. In this stage it does not: from tick 800 of a life on, the poison bushes are good and the good ones poison. A teacher that only speaks when it hurts cannot say “this is no longer bad”, so a creature taught by pain keeps avoiding what is now its best food, and goes on eating what now hurts it until each new pain has been learned.
The new teacher is a critic. It keeps an expectation and teaches with the difference. An expected pain teaches nothing new; a pain that fails to come is a pleasant surprise, and that undoes the aversion.

title: Critic
text:
The dopamine cell fires at a steady resting rate. Its rate minus that rest is the surprise: above it, things went better than expected; below it, worse. Taste excites it, through its relay cell (us_taste); pain, through its own (us_pain), excites the habenula, which silences it.
Value cells in the ventral striatum read the pallium and learn, within the life, how good (value_app) and how bad (value_av) the next moments will be when a bush looks like this. Like all striatal cells they inhibit. The good ones learn from bursts, the bad ones from pauses: the two learning rules of the striatum’s two cell types.
Each prediction reaches the dopamine cell twice. Fast, through steadily active cells of the pallidum that it inhibits (ventral_pallidum, gp_habenular): a rising good prediction releases dopamine at once, a rising bad one releases the habenula. And slowly, directly, a moment late. Fast minus slow is the change of prediction, so the surprise is taste − pain + prediction now − prediction a moment ago: when things go as predicted, the terms cancel.
The surprise teaches the value cells, so the predictions improve, and the synapses from the look and the pallium onto the cells of appetite and aversion: a good surprise strengthens the appetite for what is in view and weakens the aversion to it, a bad surprise the other way round.

title: Critic
text:
Biology
Dopamine cells in the midbrain fire a burst when something turns out better than expected and pause when it turns out worse. In the classic recordings in monkeys they fire at a drop of juice; once a light reliably announces the juice, they fire at the light instead; and when the juice is then left out, they pause at the moment it should have come. This is the teaching signal of temporal-difference learning, a method from machine learning that predicted these recordings.
How the expectation is subtracted is the work of the basal ganglia. The ventral striatum (nucleus accumbens) learns what a sight predicts and reaches the dopamine cells in two ways: directly, with slow inhibition, and through the ventral pallidum, whose steady inhibition of the dopamine cells it lifts. Bad news takes a parallel route through a part of the pallidum that drives the habenula, which pauses the dopamine cells; it was described in the lamprey, the oldest living vertebrate line. The same striatum, pallidum and dopamine signal will later choose actions.
Insects run the same scheme in the mushroom body (the counterpart of the pallium), with separate dopamine cells for reward and for punishment. Mammals mostly signal both with one population of cells, as this model does.

title: Critic
text:
The world
The world of the pallium stage made harder, so that learning cannot be done without. A bush carries a single berry, and a poison berry costs as much food as a good one gives: biting every bush once to see gains nothing, only judging a bush by its look does. Meals are small and the body burns slowly, so one bad bite never kills and a creature has time for many lessons. For the first half of the evolution the kinds keep their meaning; from then on, at tick 800 of every life, the two poison kinds of bush turn good and the two good kinds turn poison, their looks unchanged.

title: Critic
text:
Did it work?



The critic pays, alone and when the two kinds share a world. Without learning half the fitness is lost: in this world a creature that does not learn which bushes hurt cannot live. Almost all of that is the learned aversion; the learned appetite helps a little in one of the three lineages. Of the critic’s cells, those that predict bad things (value_av) are used; those that predict good things (value_app) are not. The critic’s lesson here is “this no longer hurts”: a pain that was predicted and does not come.



After the switch only the critic’s creatures take up the new food. Early in life both kinds of creature bite the bushes that hurt less often than the good ones. After tick 800 both soon stop eating the bushes that turned poison, since every bite of them hurts. But the bushes that turned good are another matter: the critic’s creatures eat more and more of them, while the pain teacher’s go on avoiding them, held back by an aversion nothing in them can undo.

In the lab
The theory makes sharp predictions, and they can be tested on one creature at a time. A new bush is put in front of it; it bites three times and feels pain each time; after a pause the next trial begins.



The surprise moves to the warning. At the first painful meal the signal drops at the bites. After a few meals it also drops as soon as the bush appears. When the pain is then left out, the signal turns positive where the pain should have been, as in the monkey recordings. Unlike in those recordings, the drop at the bites shrinks only a little: the critic learns that the bush hurts, not when. Nothing the creature senses changes between seeing the bush and biting it, so the prediction of a moment ago and the one now mostly cancel each other at the bite. A sense of time since a warning is for a later stage.



Extinction: when the pain stops, the critic’s aversion fades away over twelve meals (in one seed it even falls below zero); the pain teacher’s does not change at all, since nothing in it can weaken a lesson.

title: Critic
text:
Full results






NoteFitness over the generations








The kinds swap within a life from generation 50 on; until then each kind keeps its meaning, and fitness falls for both at the change.









NoteAll fitness measures

















NoteAll lesions








The large losses for dopamine, habenula, ventral_pallidum and gp_habenular show that the circuit is needed, but their size is not a measure of use alone. These cells are steadily active, and the surprise is measured against their resting rates: silencing one of them leaves a surprise that never settles at zero, and it unteaches or overteaches every lesson.









NoteThe lab and the switch in numbers








Blocking (last two rows) is a test of the theory: a second warning sign, added to one that already predicts the pain, should be learned less than one added to a sign that predicted nothing. The critic shows a small effect in that direction; the pain teacher none.












NoteWhat it took






A world where the look matters. In the first version of this stage (the pallium’s world, six berries to a bush, reversal from the start) neither kind of creature judged a bush by its look before biting: they bit every bush once and stopped if it hurt. The critic paid there only by a learned appetite for bushes in general. A learned aversion was there, but too weak to stop a bite: one painful bite is one tick of pain, and the lesson stayed below what the aversive cells need to fire. Evolution then turned the aversion learning down.
A harsh world, with room for mistakes. A poison bite costing as much as a good one gives makes trying everything worthless. Making it dearer alone killed the creatures before they could learn; smaller meals and a slower metabolism spread the same risk over many decisions.
Learning to start with. The aversion learning starts ten times stronger than the pallium stage left it, so that the first generation has learners to select; evolution kept it high.
A calm start. With the swap from the first generation, the lesson that the look matters had to be learned in a world that keeps changing its mind; with fifty generations without it, caution by look evolves first.
Both paths. With only the slow, direct inhibition the dopamine cell compares what happens with what was predicted for this very moment. A known poison bush in view then predicts pain before any pain comes, and that reads as relief: on every step of the approach it unlearned the aversion, and the creatures did worse than with no predictions at all. The fast path through the pallidum turns the comparison into one between now and a moment ago, so a view that stays the same is no surprise.
A first version of this page computed the surprise with a formula instead of cells. The creatures did about as well with it as with these; the cells are kept because they are how the brain does it and because the basal ganglia that follow are built from the same parts.
Both sides learn. In a second version only the aversion learned from the critic, a leftover of the time when pain was the only teacher. When taste alone taught the appetite (in the association stage), the learned appetite spread to look-alike poison; with a teacher that also speaks after a bad bite, it does not. The creatures did as well either way, and the appetite stays.
Pain at its limit. A full pain drove the habenula to the top of its range, where a prediction could no longer lower it. Evolution turned the pain’s strength down to 40 to 75% of its design.
Counting the cells. Each value cell has its own synapse onto the next cell, so a prediction’s strength has to be shared out over them; at first it was not, the predictions counted three times over, and evolution damped them by pushing the horizon to its end.
The right moment. The surprise of a tick is about the step that led to it, so it changes the synapses that were active a tick earlier (real synapses are changed by dopamine that arrives a second or two late).
Steady cells keep their strength. Evolution may tune how strongly the predictions reach the dopamine cell, but not the outputs of the steadily active cells: changing those moved the dopamine cell’s resting rate, and a surprise that never settles at zero.
A short horizon. Nothing tells the creature how long a pain will last while the bush is in view, so the predictions look only a few ticks ahead. A sense of time since a warning is for a later stage.
Wiring of its own. The pallium’s random wiring belongs to the creature’s place in the population, not to its genes, so no lineage can inherit a lucky code.

title: Critic
text: Runs

title: Actor
text:
The circuit
Hands, and a circuit that chooses what they do
Until now biting a bush was eating it. In this stage the two come apart: the action USE picks a berry with an empty hand and puts it down with a full one, and EAT eats what is held. The same action now means different things in different situations, and the right one depends on what is in hand. That is the job of an actor: a circuit that learns, from the critic’s surprise, which action pays where.

title: Actor
text:
Hands. The pallium reads what is in hand as well as what is ahead, so the critic and the actor know what is held. Appetite and aversion now mean eat it and do not eat it: cells about the held berry drive and stop swallowing (ingest, no_eat), and a berry in hand is swallowed by default unless aversion stops it. The old programmes about what is seen act on eating as well; evolution may take them away entirely.
The actor has one channel per hand action, USE and EAT. In each, a Go cell (striatum_d1) and a NoGo cell (striatum_d2) read the pallium. Go inhibits the steadily active output cell (gpi), which releases the action’s programme (act); NoGo inhibits a relay (gpe) that otherwise holds gpi down, so NoGo strengthens the brake.
Learning. A dopamine burst strengthens the synapses onto Go cells that were active a moment before, a pause those onto NoGo cells. Which cells were active is marked by a copy of the action just taken, sent back to the striatum (an efference copy), so an action is credited also when an older circuit chose it.
A start. A full hand releases USE now and then, so that putting down is tried at all and can be learned. Evolution sets how often.
Nothing new for the thorns. A prick is a pain like a snake bite, felt by the pain cells the critic already reads; the brain is the same as without thorns.

title: Actor
text:
Biology
The dorsal striatum is the input of the basal ganglia. Its cells come in two kinds with two dopamine receptors. D1 cells form the direct pathway: they inhibit the output nuclei (GPi, SNr), whose steady inhibition holds the brainstem’s motor programmes shut, and so release an action. D2 cells form the indirect pathway through the external pallidum and hold it back. Dopamine bursts strengthen the active synapses onto D1 cells and pauses those onto D2 cells, so actions that turned out better than expected are released more readily and worse ones held back. With the critic of the last page this is the actor-critic of reinforcement learning, and the basal ganglia are its best-known biological counterpart.
The two pathways are old: lampreys, the oldest living vertebrate line, have them, with the same transmitters and dopamine receptors. That the striatum gets a copy of the motor command is clearest in songbirds, where a basal ganglia loop learns which variant of a song syllable was sung when the song turned out well.
Learning to leave defended prey alone is old too. Pike that snap at three-spined sticklebacks get their mouths pricked by the spines and soon stop attacking them, while still taking minnows; toads stung by a bee stop snapping at bees, and at the flies that look like them.

title: Actor
text:
The world
The critic’s harsh world, without the switch: one berry to a bush, a poison berry costing as much food as a good one gives, small meals and a slow metabolism. Eating now takes a hand: a berry must be picked, then eaten. A held berry blocks the next pick until it is eaten or put down, and it can only be put down on an empty cell.
The poison bushes have thorns (not in OHOL, though real gooseberry bushes are spiny). Picking from one pricks: a small pain and a little food lost, at the pick itself, before anything is eaten. Which kinds are poison, and so thorny, is drawn anew for every life, so it has to be learned each time.

title: Actor
text:
Did it work?



The actor pays. Creatures with it live longer well fed than creatures without it, alone and when the two kinds share a world, and less of what they eat is poison. The lead is smaller in one of the three lines, where the creatures without the actor had learned to leave the thorny bushes alone almost completely.
And they lean on its learning. Switching off the learning of the actor’s Go cells costs about a fifth of the fitness (a tenth to two fifths per line), that of the NoGo cells about a tenth. Silencing the actor’s output (act) costs a third.

In the lab
One creature at a time is put in a box, 48 times: in front of a bush with an empty hand, or with a berry in hand and nothing ahead. Which two of the four kinds are poison, and thorny, is new for every creature, so whatever it does with them after the first trials it has learned.



The actor keeps the good bushes picked. Creatures with the actor learn to leave the thorny bushes (from about seven in ten picked to four) and go on picking more than eight in ten of the good ones. With the striatum’s learning switched off they leave the thorny bushes just as well, through the cells of appetite and aversion, but the good ones come along: fewer and fewer of them are picked. The prick spreads to everything that looks like a bush, and what the actor learns, from the good berries that follow a pick, holds that back. Creatures without the actor leave the thorny bushes almost completely, but also four in ten of the good ones from the start.



A poison berry in hand is put down. At first a creature with the actor swallows a poison berry it holds; within a dozen trials it puts most of them down instead, with or without the striatum’s learning: that what is not swallowed gets put down is built in. Creatures without the actor cannot put anything down: they hold the berry, and often swallow it in the end.
Why thorns. Without them a wrong pick cost nothing the critic could see: the creature found the berry bad and put it down, a few ticks lost. The actor’s circuit was used then, but its learning was not (a few percent at most). A prick is a cost of the action itself, which the cells about eating cannot prevent: only picking less can. Thorns on every bush were tried first. They failed: a creature that cannot yet tell the kinds apart loses food on every pick, and a prick after every pick taught aversion to every colour.

title: Actor
text:
Full results






NoteFitness over the generations

















NoteAll fitness measures

















NoteAll lesions








The old programmes about what is seen (grasp, no_feed) are not needed any more. Neither is the aversion to the berry in hand (no_eat): with the poison bushes picked less, a poison berry is seldom held.









NoteThe lab in numbers

















NoteWhat it took






The berry has to tell something new. In a first version every kind’s bush, berry and empty bush shared one colour, and creatures picked and ate at once, as if eating were still biting: the berry in hand said nothing the bush had not. A world where only the berries were coloured was tried and dropped.
Valence means eating. First the cells about what is seen still worked on USE, as they had when picking was eating. A creature that had learned to dislike a poison berry in hand then could not put it down: the dislike stopped the hand. On EAT, where appetite and aversion belong, USE is the actor’s.
No switch. The critic’s world swapped poison and good kinds halfway through every life. Here a berry that is refused is never tasted again, so a dislike learned before the swap never faded, and both kinds ended up disliked. The switch was there to show the critic at work and is gone from this stage on.
A fresh start for the hands. In the critic stage the hand was always empty and EAT did nothing, so the synapses from the held senses and onto EAT had drifted unselected; they start silent. Swallowing what is held is the default, with a strength that evolves.
The right moment. The cells of appetite and aversion read the pallium of the same tick, not of the tick before: a berry is swallowed on its first tick in hand, before a lesson a tick late could stop it.
Room to remove. The connections of the old programmes that got in the way can be evolved down to nothing, not only weakened.
A cost for a wrong pick. Without one the actor’s learning was not used (the stage was first frozen so). Thorns on every bush starved the creatures at the start, at every setting tried; thorns on the poison bushes only, a small pain and a little food, let the start live and made picking by look pay.
Fifty generations, not a hundred: the difference between the two kinds was clear by generation 20 to 30.
